title: Multidimensional Anxiety Theory
body: Multidimensional anxiety theory splits competitive state anxiety into separate parts that relate to performance in different ways. Cognitive anxiety (worry, negative expectations) is predicted to have a negative linear relationship with performance: more worry, worse performance. Somatic anxiety (perceived bodily activation such as butterflies, tension, racing heart) is predicted to follow an inverted-U, so moderate levels are best. Self-confidence is predicted to relate positively and linearly to performance. Research support for these performance predictions is mixed. The components also follow different timelines: cognitive anxiety rises early and stays fairly steady before an event, while somatic anxiety stays low until shortly before the start, peaks at the start, and fades once performance begins. The CSAI-2 was built to measure these three components. In practice, the theory tells a consultant which component to target, when to intervene, and why matching the technique to the type of anxiety makes sense.
points: Predicted: cognitive anxiety negative linear with performance
Predicted: somatic anxiety inverted-U; self-confidence positive linear
Cognitive anxiety builds early; somatic anxiety spikes near the start and then dissipates
Measured with the CSAI-2; supports matching technique to anxiety type
examNote: Expect a CSAI-2 profile or anxiety log and a question about which component to prioritize or when to intervene. Don't treat moderate somatic anxiety as a problem.

title: Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF)
body: Hanin's IZOF model holds that each performer has a personal range, or zone, of emotional intensity in which they perform best. That zone can sit at low, moderate, or high intensity, so there is no universal ideal level of anxiety or arousal. Later versions of the model expanded from anxiety to a full emotional profile that includes pleasant and unpleasant emotions, each of which can be functional (helpful) or dysfunctional (harmful) for a given person. Tension or irritation may be part of one athlete's optimal profile, while calm contentment may come before another athlete's worst performances. Assessment is idiographic: athletes recall emotions before their best and worst performances, often using their own descriptors, and these zones are then checked against ratings before upcoming competitions. Interventions help the athlete move into and stay in their own zone, which might mean energizing rather than calming.
points: Optimal zones are individual and can be at any intensity
Includes pleasant and unpleasant emotions that can be functional or dysfunctional
Assessed by recalling best and worst performances, not by comparing to norms
Intervention moves the athlete toward their own zone, up or down
examNote: IZOF is usually the answer when athletes differ in their best-performance states, or when an athlete plays best while highly anxious. Watch for distractors that impose a moderate target or group norms.

title: Catastrophe Model
body: The catastrophe model (Hardy and colleagues) describes how cognitive anxiety and physiological arousal interact to affect performance. When cognitive anxiety is low, rising physiological arousal has a mild, inverted-U effect, so performance changes gradually. When cognitive anxiety is high, increasing arousal can improve performance up to a point, after which performance drops suddenly and steeply rather than tapering off: the catastrophe. The model also predicts hysteresis: once a collapse occurs, slightly lowering arousal does not restore performance along the same path. In practice, recovery usually means bringing arousal down well below the collapse point and dealing with worry before rebuilding toward an optimal state. The model implies that neither arousal nor cognitive anxiety is harmful in itself: cognitive anxiety can even help when arousal is low. The risk lies in combining high worry with high arousal. Research support is mixed.
points: Low cognitive anxiety: arousal has a gradual, mild effect
High cognitive anxiety: arousal past a threshold causes a sudden, large drop
Hysteresis: recovery is not a simple reversal of the collapse
In practice: lower arousal substantially, address worry, then rebuild
examNote: Look for abrupt collapses that happen only when worry is high, or an athlete whose small calming efforts fail mid-competition. The inverted-U, which ignores cognitive anxiety and predicts smooth change, is the usual distractor.

title: Directional Interpretation of Anxiety
body: Jones's directional perspective adds a second question to how much anxiety a performer feels: is it experienced as helpful or harmful? The same intensity of cognitive or somatic symptoms can be interpreted as facilitative (a pounding heart means I'm ready) or debilitative (it means I'm about to fall apart). Research using direction scales added to intensity measures such as the CSAI-2 has found that direction often separates better from poorer performers, and elite performers more often report facilitative interpretations. Self-confidence appears to help protect a facilitative reading. In assessment, measure direction as well as intensity before deciding that high anxiety is a problem. In intervention, cognitive strategies such as restructuring, self-talk, and imagery can help performers reinterpret symptoms rather than only lowering intensity, as Hanton and Jones described with elite swimmers.
points: Same intensity can be facilitative or debilitative
Direction is measured with a rating added to intensity scales
Elite performers more often interpret anxiety as facilitative
Reinterpretation can be trained; intensity reduction isn't always the goal
examNote: When high anxiety scores coexist with strong performance, or two athletes with equal anxiety perform differently, the answer usually involves assessing or changing direction.

title: Cue Utilization Theory
body: Easterbrook's cue utilization theory explains how arousal changes the range of cues a performer attends to. At low arousal, attention is broad and lets in irrelevant cues such as crowd noise or the scoreboard, so the performer is easily distracted. As arousal rises to a moderate level, attention narrows and irrelevant cues drop out, which improves performance. If arousal keeps rising, attention narrows further and relevant cues, often peripheral ones like an open teammate or a second threat, begin to be missed, and performance declines. The theory offers one explanation for the inverted-U pattern between arousal and performance. Practically, it implies raising activation for under-aroused, distractible performers, lowering it for over-aroused ones, and training scanning of relevant cues under gradually increasing stress.
points: Low arousal: attention too broad, irrelevant cues get in
Moderate arousal: irrelevant cues are filtered out (helpful)
High arousal: relevant cues are lost too (harmful)
Adjust arousal in either direction to restore the best attentional width
examNote: Missing a relevant peripheral cue only under peak pressure points to over-narrowing; noticing everything except the task in a low-stakes moment points to under-arousal.

title: Nideffer's Attentional Styles
body: Nideffer describes attention along two dimensions: width (broad to narrow) and direction (external to internal). Together they produce four types of focus, each suited to a different demand. Broad-external focus assesses the environment quickly, as when a point guard reads the defense. Broad-internal focus analyzes and plans, as when choosing a strategy. Narrow-internal focus rehearses or centers, such as feeling a movement or taking a calming breath. Narrow-external focus locks onto a target for execution, such as the rim or the ball. Effective performers shift between these types as the situation changes; problems arise when someone gets stuck in the wrong type, such as analyzing at the moment of execution or ruminating internally while missing information around them. The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS) was developed to assess attentional tendencies.
points: Broad-external: assess the situation
Broad-internal: analyze and plan
Narrow-internal: rehearse or center
Narrow-external: execute on a target; TAIS assesses attentional style
examNote: Items describe a performer stuck in one focus and ask which shift a routine or refocusing cue should train. Match the focus type to the demand of that moment.

title: Achievement Goal Theory and Motivational Climate
body: Achievement goal theory explains motivation by how people define success. With a task orientation, success means improving, learning, and giving effort, judged against one's own past performance. With an ego orientation, success means beating others or doing as well with less effort. The orientations are independent, so a person can be high in both. The most vulnerable profile is high ego orientation with low perceived ability: when winning is the only route to feeling competent and the person doubts they can win, they tend to avoid challenges, withdraw effort, and drop out. A strong task orientation tends to protect motivation. The motivational climate created by coaches and leaders also matters. A task-involving (mastery) climate recognizes individual improvement, effort, and cooperation; an ego-involving (performance) climate emphasizes public comparison, rankings, and praise mainly for top performers. Orientation is often measured with the TEOSQ.
points: Task orientation: self-referenced improvement; ego orientation: beating others
High ego plus low perceived ability is the highest-risk profile
Mastery climate: improvement, effort, and cooperation are recognized
Performance climate: rankings, comparison, and results-only praise
examNote: Coach-behavior vignettes usually test climate (what to change), while athlete-profile vignettes test orientation plus perceived ability (who is at risk). Assess both the person and the environment.

title: Self-Determination Theory
body: Self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci) proposes three basic psychological needs: autonomy (feeling volitional and having a say), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected and cared for). Satisfying these needs supports more autonomous motivation and well-being; thwarting them pushes motivation toward control or amotivation. Motivation falls along a continuum: amotivation, external regulation (rewards and punishments), introjected regulation (guilt, shame, ego pressure), identified regulation (valuing the outcome), integrated regulation (fully aligned with one's identity), and intrinsic motivation (doing it for the activity itself). Cognitive evaluation theory, part of SDT, explains why expected tangible rewards that feel controlling can undermine intrinsic interest, whereas informational feedback can support competence. In practice, consultants and coaches use autonomy support: offering choices within limits, giving rationales, acknowledging feelings, and inviting input.
points: Needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness
Continuum: amotivation → external → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic
Controlling rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
Autonomy support: choice within limits, rationale, acknowledgment, input
examNote: Identify the regulation type from a quote (guilt means introjected), or find which need is unmet and match the fix to it. Rewards and pressure are common distractors.

title: Self-Efficacy and Its Sources
body: In Bandura's social cognitive theory, self-efficacy is a person's belief in their capability to carry out a specific task in a specific situation. It predicts choice, effort, persistence, and performance. Efficacy draws on four main sources. Performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) are the strongest. Vicarious experience, watching others succeed, has the most impact when the model is similar to the observer, and a coping model who struggles and then succeeds can be especially helpful for fearful learners. Verbal persuasion is weaker and loses credibility when it contradicts experience. Physiological and emotional states matter through how they are interpreted: a racing heart read as incapacity lowers efficacy. Sport researchers have also emphasized imaginal experiences. Collective efficacy, a group's shared belief in its joint capability, develops from the same sources, especially shared mastery.
points: Mastery experiences are the strongest source
Vicarious experience works best with similar models
Verbal persuasion is weaker and must be credible
Physiological states matter through interpretation; collective efficacy is the group-level version
examNote: If persuasion or modeling has failed, the answer is usually graded mastery experiences. For bodily signals, look for reinterpretation rather than more encouragement.

title: Attribution Theory
body: Attribution theory, especially Weiner's model, explains how the causes people give for success and failure shape their emotions, expectations, and future effort. Attributions vary on three main dimensions. Locus of causality (internal or external) is tied mainly to pride and self-esteem. Stability (stable or unstable) shapes expectations of future success: stable causes for failure predict more failure. Controllability (controllable or uncontrollable) shapes emotions such as guilt or shame and willingness to keep trying. Explaining failure with an internal, stable, uncontrollable cause, such as lack of natural ability, is linked to low expectations, reduced effort, and helplessness. Attribution retraining helps performers explain setbacks with unstable, controllable causes such as effort, strategy, and preparation. Consultants and coaches can guide attributions in debriefs by steering discussion toward factors the person or team can change.
points: Dimensions: locus of causality, stability, controllability
Stability drives future expectancy
Internal, stable, uncontrollable failure attributions are most damaging
Retraining shifts attributions toward effort and strategy
examNote: Classify a quote on the three dimensions, then pick the response that moves failure attributions toward controllable, changeable causes. Blaming luck or officials is a tempting but unhelpful distractor.

title: Vealey's Sport-Confidence Model
body: Vealey defined sport confidence as an athlete's belief or degree of certainty about their ability to be successful in sport. Her original model separated trait sport confidence (a general disposition) from state sport confidence (confidence in a particular moment) and included competitive orientation, meaning whether an athlete defines success by performing well or by winning. Trait confidence and competitive orientation were proposed to shape state confidence, which in turn influences performance. Later work took a multidimensional approach and identified sources of sport confidence, including mastery, demonstration of ability, physical and mental preparation, physical self-presentation, social support, vicarious experience, coaches' leadership, environmental comfort, and situational favorableness. Sources athletes control, such as mastery and preparation, are thought to give a sturdier foundation than sources that depend on others' evaluations or on circumstances. Consultants help athletes broaden confidence toward these controllable sources and reconnect with evidence of their preparation.
points: Trait vs. state sport confidence; competitive orientation
Later work identified multiple sources of sport confidence
Controllable sources (mastery, preparation) are thought to be sturdier
Confidence that relies on others' approval tends to be fragile
examNote: Vignettes describe confidence that swings with feedback, results, or disrupted training. The best answer rebuilds it from mastery and preparation rather than more praise or lower goals.

title: Cohesion, the GEQ, Group Development, and Shared Mental Models
body: Carron describes cohesion as a dynamic process, seen in a group's tendency to stay together while pursuing its goals and meeting members' needs. Task cohesion concerns working together toward goals; social cohesion concerns liking one another. The Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ) measures four parts: individual attractions to the group–task and –social, and group integration–task and –social. Interpret each dimension separately; high social cohesion does not offset low task cohesion. Team building targets task cohesion with shared goals, role clarity, and standards, and in exercise groups with distinctiveness, norms, and member interaction. Tuckman's model of group development runs forming, storming (conflict over roles and influence), norming, and performing, with adjourning added later for groups that disband. Shared mental models, team members' overlapping knowledge of roles, cues, and procedures, support coordination and are built through briefs, rehearsal, and debriefs.
points: Task vs. social cohesion; GEQ: ATG-T, ATG-S, GI-T, GI-S
Team building: goals, roles, norms, distinctiveness, interaction
Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
Shared mental models drive coordination among skilled individuals
examNote: Read GEQ profiles by dimension, recognize storming as normal rather than failure, and choose shared-mental-model work when skilled individuals coordinate poorly.

title: Resilience and Stress Appraisal
body: Lazarus's transactional model holds that stress comes from appraisal, not from demands alone. Primary appraisal asks what is at stake; secondary appraisal asks whether one's coping resources are adequate. Demands appraised as exceeding resources produce threat and distress; demands seen as manageable can be appraised as challenges. This explains why two people facing identical demands respond differently, and it points interventions toward both the meaning of the demand and the person's resources. Fletcher and Sarkar's grounded theory of resilience in Olympic champions found that psychological factors (positive personality, motivation, confidence, focus, and perceived social support) protected performers from the potential negative effects of stressors, partly by promoting challenge appraisals and helpful meta-cognitions. Resilience is a process that can be developed; their later work on mental fortitude training emphasizes manageable challenge combined with support, not removing all adversity.
points: Primary appraisal: what's at stake; secondary appraisal: can I cope
Same demands, different appraisals, different stress
Protective psychological factors promote challenge appraisals
Resilience develops through challenge with support
examNote: If people face equal demands but respond differently, the answer involves appraisal. For resilience programs, reject options that remove all stressors or treat resilience as a fixed trait.
